The central question is: given a stream of incoming examples with shifting feature distributions and shifting label marginals, how do you set your drift detector's sensitivity so that it catches real concept drift fast enough to matter operationally, without flooding the retraining pipeline with false alarms triggered by benign variance or seasonal cycles? The key concepts in tension are detection delay (how many post-drift samples you consume before triggering) and false positive rate (how often you fire on stable data), mediated by the detector's window size and threshold — and the non-stationary label distribution adds a third axis: when P(Y) itself shifts, feature-conditional drift detectors like ADWIN or DDM can misattribute label imbalance changes as covariate shift, producing false alarms that are statistically defensible but operationally meaningless. What a beginner misses is that the tradeoff is asymmetric in cost: a false positive wastes compute and can destabilize a model that was performing fine (triggering retraining on insufficient new data often hurts accuracy), while a false negative lets a degraded model serve predictions silently — and the dominant failure mode in production is not one or the other but alarm fatigue, where operators suppress or ignore detectors entirely after too many false positives, eliminating the safety net. Experts also worry about detector-induced feedback loops: if your drift detector gates label collection (e.g., you only request ground truth after an alarm), then under non-stationary label distributions your detector's training signal is itself corrupted by the selection bias it created, making recalibration unreliable precisely when you need it most.

A concrete design choice that partially breaks this circularity is to monitor the output distribution of a separately trained, frozen reference model (trained on the reference window and never updated), so your drift statistic isn't coupled to the operational model's degradation trajectory; Lipton et al. When you scan a candidate reference window with a sliding sub-window test — say, KS applied at every position with stride s over a window of length N — you're conducting O(N/s) hypothesis tests on overlapping, autocorrelated samples, which means naive Bonferroni correction drastically over-penalizes (requiring p < 0.05·s/N per test) while ignoring the autocorrelation makes your family-wise error rate (FWER) wildly optimistic; the practical result is that either you reject valid reference windows too aggressively or you pass contaminated ones. The interaction with minimum window size is a hard squeeze: your downstream detector — say, MMD with a Gaussian kernel — needs roughly N ≥ 500–1000 samples per class to achieve 80% power at a 5% significance level for moderate effect sizes (δ ≈ 0.3 in standardized feature space), but increasing N to satisfy power requirements means your stability scan covers more sub-windows and accumulates more multiple comparisons, requiring stricter per-test thresholds that are harder to satisfy on the same N samples. The statistically correct framework here is the scan statistic literature (Kulldorff 1997; Siegmund & Yakir 2000), which computes the maximum of a test statistic over all sub-windows and derives its null distribution via Monte Carlo permutation rather than applying pointwise thresholds — this controls FWER exactly while accounting for autocorrelation, but costs O(N²) comparisons and requires 10³–10⁴ permutation draws, which is computationally prohibitive for online recertification cycles running every few minutes. A practical approximation used in production systems like Arize and Fiddler is block bootstrap: resample contiguous blocks of length √N to preserve local autocorrelation structure, compute the scan statistic on each bootstrap replicate, and use the 95th percentile of the bootstrap distribution as your rejection threshold — this reduces the permutation cost by ~10× while maintaining reasonable FWER control for weakly dependent streams. The deeper tension is that the window size that satisfies detector power is not the same window size that minimizes scan statistic variance: short windows have low power but few multiple comparisons; long windows have high power but the scan statistic's null distribution widens because there are more opportunities to observe a spurious maximum, meaning your certification threshold must grow with N in a way that partially cancels the power gain you sought by increasing N in the first place.

With weekly seasonality, the covariance between observations at lag τ decays as ~cos(2πτ/168) rather than exponentially, meaning blocks separated by less than one full period (168 hours for hourly data) carry strong residual dependence — resampling such blocks as if they were independent understates the variance of your scan statistic by a factor that scales with the ratio of the effective sample size N_eff to N, which Lahiri (2003) shows can be as large as 5–20× for moderate seasonality strength. The concrete FWER failure mode is threshold deflation: your bootstrap null distribution is too narrow because the resampled pseudo-streams don't reproduce the full periodic variance structure, so your 95th percentile rejection threshold is set too low, and the scan statistic on real data — which does express the full seasonal swing — exceeds it routinely even under the null, inflating false positive rates far above the nominal 5%. For user session structure, the problem is compounded by within-session autocorrelation that operates at a different timescale than the between-session periodicity: a single user session may span 10–50 requests with highly correlated feature vectors, creating a two-level dependence hierarchy that no single block length ℓ can simultaneously capture — short blocks miss inter-session periodicity, long blocks fail to respect session boundaries and mix sessions artificially. A subtler failure is sensitivity inversion: because the amplitude break reduces seasonal variance, the remainder after decomposition actually becomes smaller in magnitude during the early break phase (the shrinking seasonal signal is partially attributed to a reduced seasonal estimate), temporarily making the stream look more stable to your detector exactly when it is becoming less so. The concrete bias is upward inflation of AR coefficients toward unit-root territory: for a linear ramp of slope δ over N observations, the bias in the lag-1 Yule-Walker estimate is approximately δ²N/(6σ²), which for moderate ramps (δ = 0.1σ per period over N=50 periods) pushes ρ̂₁ upward by roughly 0.08–0.15 — enough to meaningfully over-smooth the pre-whitening filter and leave residual low-frequency structure in the output.
